title: How much the tunes themselves mattered
summary: They discuss New Orleans versus Chicago-written tunes, built-in discipline of a standard repertoire, and martial brass-band tempo.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: They're a relief of what might be, Manon. Yeah. The question, you bring up something here, the question of the importance of the tune. We have a great affection for the New Orleans repertoire, the Dixieland tunes, and the Dixieland revivalists have a great affection for them, and even the Chicagoans have a great affection for them. Do you think that the tune might also have been important in making jazz a New Orleans derivative? Do you think that, if without Dixieland tunes, that there might have been a Dixieland style?

If you analyze the tunes that the Wolverines played, presumably unaffected, you'll find that when they play Royal Garden or Jasmine Blues, those are the weakest things they played. And they played them totally different from New Orleans. When they play a tune like Need Some Padding or Susie, which were written in Chicago, the band plays infinitely better.
So a tune can have a relationship.

Oh, a great relationship. Where the New Orleans tunes had a big effect, the biggest one, I think, really, is the fact that a band that's never played together can sound perfectly fine on Muscat Ramble because it's predetermined what you're going to do. There's enough discipline and plan to it. So without anything written, it's a well thought out, integrated type of performance. Whereas, you ask them to start just a group that's never played together, they ask them to play a tune. They have no way of knowing how it's going to come out.

There's a great individuality, individual difference, in the approach of musicians to repertoire. Bud used to like to play to an empty house on new tunes. This was fun, to play new tunes. Of course, it's just rehearsal, or what amounts to. But if one were inclined to be at all lazy, why just play old tunes and repeat them?

They play themselves. Yeah. The other factor, I mentioned that there were two, is the fact that there's a martial aspect to it. Yes. The thing that makes people step quickly along beside a brass band is the same effect that the New Orleans tunes always had, because they originated in brass bands. And that is an inspiring sort of thing. It quickens the tempo.

Well, and as you said before, if blues is the second great reservoir of repertoire, the slowest tempos deriving from the blues also are characteristically New Orleans. And the show tunes and the Chicago tunes and so forth can find a middle tempo, don't they?
